XVIII.|OF THE APOSTLES.|345}}</noinclude>either to be adored with godly honour, or to be any resemblance of the Diuinitie or any of the three persons in Godhead, but only of Christ as he was in forme of man, who in that respect may be truely expressed, as other men by their purtraites: and of the Holy Ghost, not as he is in him self, but as he appeared in firy tongues or in the similitude of a dooue, or such like. {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=How there may be Images or resemblances of the thre persons in Trinitie, and of Angels.}}And so to paint or graue any of the three persons as they appeared visibly and corporally, is no more inconuenient or vnlawful, then it vvas vndecent for them to appeare in such formes. And therfore to paint or portraite the Father also being the first person, as he hath shevved him self in vision to any of the Prophetes of the old or new Testament (namely to Daniel as an old man) {{MarginNote|margin=left|margin-width=65|text=''Dan. 7, 22.''}}or the three Angels representing the three Persons to Abraham, {{MarginNote|margin=left|margin-width=65|text=''Gen. 18, 2.''}}or the one Angel that wrastling vvith Iacob bare our Lords Person, {{MarginNote|margin=left|margin-width=65|text=''Gen. 32, 24.''}}no such thing is any vvhere forbidden, but is very agreable to the peoples instruction. In vvhich sort the Angels vvere commonly pourtered {{MarginNote|margin=left|margin-width=65|text=''Exo. 37, 7,''}}(and namely the Cherubins ouer the Propitiatorie) as they be novv in the Church, not in their natural forme, but vvith corporal vvinges (as the Seraphins appeared to Esay the Prophete) {{MarginNote|margin=left|margin-width=65|text=''Esa. 6, 2.''}}to expresse their qualitie and office of being Gods Angels, that is, ''Messengers'': and God the Father with the world in his hand, to signifie his creation and gouernement of the same, and such like: Whereof the people being vvel instructed may take much good, and no harme in the world, being now through their faith in Christ far from al fond imagination of the false gods of the Pagans. {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=Images are for the peoples instruction.}}And therfore S. Gregorie {{MarginNote|margin=left|margin-width=65|text=''Dan. 7, 22. Gen. 18, 2. Gen. 32, 24''.}}saith of the Churches Images, ''That which scripture or writing doth to the readers, the same doth the picture to the simple that looke therevpon. for in it euen the ignorant see vvhat they ought to folovv, in it they do read, that knovv no letters''. Where he calleth it a matter of antiquitie and very conuenient, that in holy places Images were painted to the peoples instruction, so they be taught that they may not be adored with diuine honour. and he in the same place sharply rebuketh Serenus the Bishop of Massilia, that of indiscrete zele he vvould take avvay Images, rather then teach the people how to vse them.

''34. Dionysius Areopagita.''] {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=S. Dionysius Areopagita is al for the Catholikes.}}This is that famous Denys that first conuerted France, and wrote those notable and diuine vvorkes ''de Ecclesiastica & cælesti hierarchia, de diuinis nominibus'', and others, in vvhich he confirmeth and proueth plainely almost al things that the Church now vseth in the ministration of the holy Sacraments, and affirmeth that he learned them of the Apostles, giuing also testimonie for the Catholike faith in most things now controuersed, so plainely, that our Aduersaries haue no shift but to deny this Denys to haue been the author of them, feyning that they be an others of later age. Vvhich is an old flight of Heretikes, but most proper to these of al others. Who seeing al antiquitie against them, are forced to be more bold or rather impudent then others in that point.

{{c|{{larger|{{sc|Chap. XVIII.}}}}}}

{{c|''At Corinth in Achaia, he worketh vvith his owne hands, preaching IESVS to be CHRIST, vnto the Iewes vpon their Sabboths. 6 But they being obstinate and blaspheming, he in plaine termes forsaketh them, and turneth to the Gentils, among whom according to a vision that he had to embolden him, he planteth the Church in great numbers, 12 the obstinat Iewes in vaine soliciting the Proconsul against him. 18 From thence at length departing he returneth 19 by Ephesus (where he promiseth the Iewes to returne to them) 22 and so to Antioch in Syria (from whence he began his iourney Act. 15) 23 but not resting, by and by he goeth againe to visite the new Churches that he planted Act. 16 in Galatia and Phrygia: 24 Apollo in his absence mightily confounding the Iewes at Ephesus, 27 and afterward at Corinth.''}} {{dropinitial|A|image=Rhemes New Testament 1582 initial A, a bearded man.png|imgsize=115px|fl={{verse|chapter=18|verse=1}}}}FTER these things, departing from Athens, he came to Corinth. {{verse|chapter=18|verse=2}}† and finding a certaine Iew, named Aquila, borne in Pontus, vvho of late vvas come out of Italie, and Priscilla his vvife (because Claudius had commaunded al Iewes to depart from Rome,) he came to them. {{verse|chapter=18|verse=3}}† And because he vvas of the same craft, he remained with them, and wrought, (and they vvere tentmakers by their craft.) {{verse|chapter=18|verse=4}}† And<noinclude>{{rh||Xx|he}}</noinclude>
